For your information:
This document is a Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) case study, not malware analysis or threat intelligence on a single malware family. It compares two real ransomware incidents to demonstrate one central lesson:
The speed of incident response is often the biggest factor determining whether ransomware encrypts an organization or is stopped before impact.
Executive Summary
Talos compares two organizations that experienced remarkably similar attacks:
Engagement 1Engagement 2Chaos ransomware affiliateMedusa ransomware affiliateCustomer engaged Talos immediatelyCustomer ignored alertsTalos received immediate accessTalos got access ~30+ hours later0% encryptionNearly 100% encryption
Talos concludes that response time—not attacker sophistication—was the dominant reason for the dramatically different outcomes.
Main Research Question
The article investigates:
Does engaging IR early materially reduce ransomware impact?
Their answer is:
Yes.
The attackers, tools, techniques, and environment were very similar.
The response timing was different.
Engagement 1
Initial Access
The attackers used
Email bombing
Microsoft Teams impersonation
Fake IT support
Microsoft Quick Assist
to socially engineer the victim.
This is becoming a common modern initial access technique.
What they did
The attackers performed classic ransomware preparation:
Discovery
AD enumeration
Lateral movement
Password changes
Remote desktop
Reverse SSH tunnels
RMM deployment
Data exfiltration
Attempted encryption
Talos lists commands like
ipconfig /all
nltest /dclist
quser.exe
and reverse SSH
ssh.exe -R ...
They also used
AnyDesk
OptiTune
ScreenConnect
SplashTop
Quick Assist
Rclone
These are all legitimate administrative tools abused by attackers.
Outcome
Talos was called before ransomware executed.
Because of that:
logs still existed
attackers had not completed preparation
defenders removed access
encryption never occurred
Result:
Data theft but no ransomware encryption.
Engagement 2
This attack was almost identical.
Differences:
The customer
ignored MDR alerts
delayed IR engagement
delayed network access for Talos
During that time:
ransomware deployed
logs deleted
shadow copies removed
systems encrypted
Result:
Nearly every endpoint encrypted.
Interesting Technical Observations
The Medusa operators used
SimpleHelp
instead of AnyDesk.
Talos observed:
Brute Ratel activity
JWrapper
PsExec
vssadmin
registry modification
System32 access
UAC disabling
Example:
vssadmin delete shadows
Classic
MITRE
T1490
(Inhibit System Recovery).
Talos' Core Finding
Talos explicitly states:
The difference was NOT
malware quality
actor sophistication
endpoint product
tooling
It was
timeliness of response.
Why logs matter
One excellent point in the paper:
If responders arrive early,
they can still recover
PowerShell history
Event logs
Process execution
Authentication logs
Registry modifications
Lateral movement path
If responders arrive late,
attackers often delete
Event logs
PowerShell history
Temp artifacts
which dramatically reduces forensic visibility.
Defensive Recommendations
Talos recommends:
Educate users against phishing and social engineering.
Restrict and monitor PowerShell and administrative tools.
Protect and retain logs (e.g., Sysmon and centralized logging).
Restrict unauthorized RMM software.
Use DLP controls to reduce data exfiltration.
Reset passwords after compromise and strengthen identity controls.
Why this document is valuable for NivXRay
From the perspective of your platform, this article is effectively a real-world validation corpus rather than just a blog post. It contains rich analyst data that can be converted into deterministic knowledge.
Some high-value items you can extract include:
Command chains: ipconfig, nltest, quser, wmic, vssadmin, ssh.exe, PsExec, PowerShell, etc.
LOLBAS patterns: WMIC, PsExec, PowerShell, OpenSSH, vssadmin.
RMM abuse: Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, SimpleHelp, Splashtop, OptiTune.
MITRE ATT&CK mappings: Discovery, Lateral Movement, Command and Control, Impact, Inhibit System Recovery, Persistence.
Attack progression: Initial Access → Discovery → Lateral Movement → Persistence → Exfiltration → Impact.
Behavioral rules: "Social engineering + Quick Assist + RMM installation + AD discovery + shadow copy deletion" is a strong ransomware precursor pattern.
Threat indicators: File hashes, domains, IPs, and filenames for both Chaos and Medusa campaigns.
Overall assessment
This is a high-quality operational incident response study. Rather than introducing new malware techniques, it demonstrates how real ransomware operations unfold and highlights that rapid detection and response can be more decisive than the specific ransomware family used. For a platform like NivXRay, it is especially valuable as a source of realistic command sequences, attack chains, LOLBAS usage, and deterministic behavioral patterns that can enrich your decoder, DKP, Attack Story, and future validation corpus.
